html:
Safia Iqbal, 17, hadn’t seen her weight in months.

Diagnosed with anorexia nervosa, she and her mother knew how quickly seeing her weight could trigger a spiral.

On the advice of their therapist, her mother, Hafsa Iqbal, had removed the scale from their home. This precautionary step, endorsed by a growing number of eating disorder specialists, had helped.

The summer before her senior year, Iqbal chose to take another step in her recovery by entering a Renfrew outpatient treatment facility.

But the Renfrew staff, without her mother’s knowledge or approval, had shown Iqbal her weight and on her sixth day in the program, she learned she had gained 3.5 pounds.

She was gutted.

That afternoon, she went home and swallowed 16 Prozac pills.

Iqbal’s suicide attempt reveals the devastating stakes when eating disorder care goes wrong. Despite her well-documented medical history, The Renfrew Center — a national for-profit network that promises patient recovery  — missed the warning signs which culminated in a teenager’s suicide attempt.

Then, in an apparent effort to cover its tracks, employees sought to backdate Iqbal's treatment records to make it appear that she had received an individualized treatment plan when she had not, violating Renfrew's own “key components of care”.

An estimated 28 million people struggle with an eating disorder in the United States. Eating disorders have the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric condition, with one death occurring nearly every hour. Yet eating disorders remain deeply misunderstood, difficult to treat, and under-researched.

The Renfrew Center, a pioneer in the field of eating disorder treatment, has become one of the most influential eating disorder treatment centers in the United States. Based in Philadelphia, they have XX facilities in XX states and claim to have treated 100,000 people over the last 40 years. Renfrew influences how treatment is delivered far beyond its own centers. Its top executives hold positions on several of the key boards that govern the eating disorder treatment industry. Renfrew also holds an influential annual conference featuring celebrity speakers, and offers training sessions for students and medical professionals. In many ways, Renfrew’s model for eating disorder treatment has become the blueprint others follow.

But there’s a problem.

Documents including personal journals and medical records, along with interviews with former patients and former employees, reveal account after account where patients left The Renfrew Center worse than they went in.

attrs.caption: All I really experienced there was people telling me what I was doing wrong and it just adds a new level of shame
attrs.cite: Brenna Hallman, former patient at a Renfrew facility

html:
Our investigation found a pattern of contradictions between Renfrew’s promises and its practices. In its marketing materials and its website, Renfrew promises individualized, evidence-based care delivered by highly trained staff in a safe and supportive environment. But former employees and patients described an environment beset by chronic understaffing, inadequate training and rigid one-size-fits-all approach to treatment. They described adults being treated alongside adolescents, who experts say require a different therapeutic approach. They described patients with radically different eating disorders requiring radically different treatment approaches being lumped together in identical treatment regimes. And they described a system of treatment that relied heavily on shame, isolation, and other forms of punishment.

Renfrew’s shortcomings are especially consequential because the eating disorder industry is barely regulated at all.

Fueled by growing demand and expanded insurance coverage, the eating-disorder treatment industry has grown into a multi-billion-dollar business, with nearly 400 treatment centers now operating across the country. Yet unlike traditional hospitals, eating-disorder treatment facilities that do not accept Medicaid, such as The Renfrew Center, are not subject to federal oversight. Instead, most are governed by private accreditation bodies that can substitute for state regulation and are largely shielded from public records laws.

According to experts, the result is a mostly self-regulated industry that lacks accountability.

attrs.caption: I was so scared. I was having panic attacks nonstop. I had to unlearn everything that I learned at Renfrew to then start my recovery journey again
attrs.cite: Rebecca Lebo, former patient at a Renfrew facility

html:
For patients like Rebecca Lebo, that lack of oversight left few options. Lebo entered Renfrew expecting the support the facility promised.

But after struggling to complete her meals, Lebo was not given individual support, but instead was punished for not adhering to the restrictive model. She said staff restricted her ability to advance through the program, isolated her to a single community room for months, and placed her in a high-surveillance bedroom known as the fishbowl.

attrs.caption: They don't offer individualized care
attrs.cite: – Former employee who spoke on the condition of anonymity

html:
She wasn’t allowed to go outdoors for nearly three months. Lebo said the loss of autonomy worsened her depression and fed suicidal thoughts, while her repeated pleas to staff for help went unanswered.

When she considered leaving, staff threatened her with a discharge against medical advice, a designation that could jeopardize insurance coverage for any future treatment at any other facility. Because of this threat, she stayed until her insurance ran out and continued to languish within the program that had promised to help her.

Renfrew promotes its model as one of the most successful for treating eating disorders, but experts told us some of its core practices - including routinely showing patients their weight - can increase anxiety, trigger relapse, and, in extreme cases, contribute to suicide attempts, as it did with Iqbal.

But some leaders at Renfrew say the harm to the patients is the patients’ fault, despite the center promising to give them the tools to emotionally regulate.

“The reason that they attempted suicide in the first place was because they didn’t have the emotional regulation skills to handle the trigger… to me, it’s got a lot to do with emotion regulation and less to do with the safety of the facility,” said Dr. Dee Ross Franklin, a previous Renfrew Center clinical training specialist who helped implement the center’s treatment model.

However, former patients describe not receiving the promised tools for recovery. Instead, they report that their emotional wellbeing was repeatedly disregarded, while the program’s exposure therapy protocols — such as “open weights” — contributed to increased self-harm. One former employee, who said she refused to show patients their weight despite protocol, argued that Renfrew’s model is overly simplistic. She called the center’s philosophy insulting because it reduces these complex diagnoses to little more than an attempt to avoid uncomfortable emotions.

Iqbal and Lebo are just two of an estimated 28 million people who struggle with an eating disorder in the United States. Eating disorders have the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric condition, with one death occurring every 52 to 54 minutes, according to the National Association of Anorexia Nervosa and Associated Disorders. Yet they remain deeply misunderstood, difficult to treat, under-researched, and often lacking consensus around what recovery should look like.

We spoke with over a dozen former patients, several former employees, researchers and advocates from across the country, each offering a different perspective on Renfrew’s system that is both widely trusted in the field and increasingly questioned.

What emerged was not a simple story of success or failure, but a for-profit model rigid enough to override individual needs — one that has harmed some patients even as others, and some clinicians, credit it with their recovery. And it is a model often treated as settled science, despite thin evidence and a field still early in understanding the disorders it treats.

And for patients like Iqbal and Lebo who the system failed, the cost was not just treatment that didn’t work. It was real life harm that set them both back years in their recovery journey.
